column1: {{c1::GraphQL}} lets clients request selected fields and related data in a query.
column2:
A GraphQL query names the fields it wants, such as a customer's name and related orders. The server still decides which fields and records the caller can access. Requesting a field is not permission to read it.
Review source

column1: Deeply nested GraphQL queries can threaten {{c1::availability}} by consuming excessive resources.
column2:
Nested relationships can require the server to do much more work than a short query suggests. Too much work can slow or block service for other users. Authentication proves identity but does not make every query inexpensive.
Review source

column1: Model Context Protocol lets AI agents discover and call {{c1::tools}}.
column2:
MCP gives clients a common way to discover tools and call their defined operations. In a database service, a tool can expose an approved query or procedure. MCP support alone does not grant unrestricted SQL access.
Review source

column1: {{c1::Prompt injection}} uses untrusted instructions to try to redirect an AI agent's behavior.
column2:
An agent can encounter instructions inside untrusted text, such as retrieved content. Those instructions can try to make it misuse its tools. Enforce database permissions outside the model so that an instruction cannot grant additional access.
Review source

column1: Authentication establishes identity. {{c1::Authorization}} determines permitted data and operations.
column2:
Authorization checks whether the caller has access to a specific operation and resource. Data API builder (DAB) can limit entities, actions, fields, and rows. A successfully authenticated user can still receive an access denial.
Review source

column1: DAB places authentication configuration under {{c1::runtime.host.authentication}}.
column2:
Read the dotted path as nested JSON objects: runtime contains host, which contains authentication. Put the provider and token configuration inside that authentication object. A top-level authentication object is not the documented location.
Review source

column1: DAB's {{c1::EntraID}} provider validates Microsoft Entra JWT bearer tokens.
column2:
EntraID selects DAB's Microsoft Entra bearer-token validation provider. AzureAD remains a documented compatibility name. Token validation and entity permissions are separate parts of securing the API.
Review source

column1: DAB's JWT {{c1::audience}} identifies the API that the token is intended for.
column2:
A token's audience identifies the service it is intended for. DAB validates the incoming token against its configured API audience. A token intended for SQL database access is not automatically a valid token for the DAB API.
Review source

column1: DAB's JWT {{c1::issuer}} identifies the trusted token issuer.
column2:
A JWT is a signed token containing identity information. Its issuer identifies the authority that issued it, such as a specific Entra tenant. DAB checks that issuer against its configured trusted value.
Review source

column1: With JWT bearer authentication, {{c1::X-MS-API-ROLE}} selects a custom DAB role.
column2:
The header chooses the custom role used for this request. DAB also requires that role in the token's roles claim, which lists authorized role memberships. A caller cannot gain a role merely by typing its name in the header.
Review source

column1: A valid bearer-token request without a role-selection header uses DAB's {{c1::Authenticated}} role.
column2:
DAB assigns the Authenticated system role when a valid bearer-token request has no role-selection header. It then evaluates that role's effective permissions on the requested entity. A valid token does not imply full database access.
Review source

column1: To require authentication for a DAB entity, do not grant its read action to {{c1::Anonymous}}.
column2:
Grant the read action to Authenticated or authorized custom roles, but not Anonymous. Authentication configuration alone does not remove an anonymous grant. In DAB 2.0, also review inherited permissions when assessing the entity's effective access.
Review source

column1: In DAB 2.0, an unconfigured named role first falls back to {{c1::Authenticated}} permissions for the entity.
column2:
The permission fallback order is named role, Authenticated, then Anonymous. This avoids repeating permission blocks in DAB 2.0. It does not remove the requirement for a selected custom role to appear in the caller's token.
Review source

column1: DAB controls GraphQL schema discovery with runtime.graphql.{{c1::allow-introspection}}.
column2:
allow-introspection controls whether clients can inspect the GraphQL schema. The setting is inside runtime.graphql in the configuration. Even when it is false, known queries still require proper entity and field permissions.
Review source

column1: DAB's runtime.graphql.{{c1::depth-limit}} caps query nesting.
column2:
depth-limit restricts how many levels of related fields a GraphQL query can request. The documented default is null, which imposes no depth limit. Set an appropriate explicit limit instead of assuming authentication limits query cost.
Review source

column1: DAB's runtime.pagination.{{c1::max-page-size}} caps records in one page.
column2:
max-page-size limits how many records a single page can return. It does not limit the number of bytes in each record. It also does not prevent an authorized caller from requesting another page.
Review source

column1: For a DAB table entity, the {{c1::read}} action grants reads without directly granting table writes.
column2:
The read action permits reading a table entity without directly granting create, update, or delete on it. This says nothing about the same role's access to other entities. Executable stored procedures also need review before calling the entire API read-only.
Review source

column1: A DAB action's fields.{{c1::include}} lists fields that the action permits.
column2:
fields.include names the fields permitted for that action. For example, a read action can permit OrderID and Status. This is a server-side restriction, not a suggestion about what the client requests.
Review source

column1: A DAB action's fields.{{c1::exclude}} identifies fields that the action must not expose.
column2:
fields.exclude names fields that the action must not expose. For example, InternalNotes can be excluded from a read action. Removing that field only from sample client queries does not enforce the same restriction.
Review source

column1: The DAB read policy @item.IsPublic {{c1::eq}} true restricts results to public items.
column2:
@item.IsPublic refers to the current entity row, and eq means equality in the policy language. Put the expression in the read action's policy.database property. It is an API policy expression, not a literal T-SQL WHERE clause.
Review source

column1: DAB database policies do not support {{c1::execute}} actions for stored procedures.
column2:
DAB database policies apply to supported table actions, not stored-procedure execute actions. A procedure must enforce its own row authorization or use suitable database controls. Publishing it as an API operation does not add that logic automatically.
Review source

column1: Before an API returns orders, it must authorize the trusted caller for the requested {{c1::CustomerID}}.
column2:
Knowing or supplying a customer ID does not prove permission to read that customer's orders. Compare the trusted caller with the access rules for the requested customer. A shared database login alone is not the end user's identity.
Review source

column1: By default, DAB connects to the database using {{c1::its own credentials}}, not the incoming API user's identity.
column2:
By default, DAB uses its own credentials when opening database connections. ORIGINAL_LOGIN() therefore identifies that shared SQL connection identity. Do not treat it as the individual human caller unless the authentication design supplies that distinction.
Review source

column1: SQL MCP Server uses DAB's {{c1::entity permissions}} across its tools.
column2:
DAB's SQL MCP Server exposes configured entities through the same authorization layer used by its other API surfaces. A tool call still needs the required entity action and must respect applicable restrictions. MCP is not a separate route around those rules.
Review source

column1: For agent access to database objects, prefer an {{c1::allowlist}} over SQL keyword denylists.
column2:
A keyword denylist checks text rather than proving the operation is authorized. It is not a substitute for limiting allowed objects and actions. Prefer defined tools and database permissions that enforce the intended behavior.
Review source

column1: An MCP agent with permission to execute a stored procedure can perform that procedure's {{c1::write operations}}.
column2:
A stored procedure can contain INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE even when direct table-write tools are unavailable. Permission to execute that procedure can therefore permit its writes. Review every callable procedure before declaring an agent read-only.
Review source

column1: Apply {{c1::least privilege}} to the database identity used by an API or agent.
column2:
Least privilege means granting only the access needed for a task. Limit the database connection identity as well as the API's role permissions. If the API is compromised, broad database rights can increase the damage.
Review source

column1: DAB SQL MCP Server's local stdio transport uses the {{c1::Simulator}} authentication provider.
column2:
The Simulator provider supports trusted local development without validating a real remote bearer token. stdio exchanges messages through the local process's input and output streams. Do not treat this mode as production HTTP authentication.
Review source

column1: DAB SQL MCP Server supports {{c1::streamable HTTP}} for standard HTTP hosting.
column2:
Streamable HTTP carries MCP messages over HTTP for hosted use. The server needs its supported authentication configuration and entity permissions. A client-side list of preferred restrictions does not enforce the server's access controls.
Review source

column1: Azure SQL Private Link provides connectivity through {{c1::a private endpoint}} inside a virtual network.
column2:
The private endpoint has an address inside the virtual network and connects privately to the Azure SQL logical server. This is different from allowing a public source IP through the server firewall. SQL authentication and authorization still apply.
Review source

column1: After establishing working private connectivity, block public Azure SQL access by disabling {{c1::public network access}}.
column2:
Private endpoint creation adds a private route but does not automatically remove public access. After private connectivity works, disable public network access on the logical server. Otherwise, a public connection route can remain available.
Review source

column1: Azure SQL's {{c1::sp_set_firewall_rule}} creates or updates a server-level IP allow rule.
column2:
The procedure creates or changes an allow rule for a source IP range at server scope. It runs in the logical server's master database with appropriate permissions. It does not create Private Link connectivity or turn public access off.
Review source

column1: App Service virtual network integration supports {{c1::outbound}} connections from the app.
column2:
Virtual network integration lets an App Service application make outbound calls into or through a virtual network. For example, the app can reach a database private endpoint. It does not make incoming requests to the app private.
Review source

column1: Fabric managed private endpoints give supported workloads {{c1::outbound private access}} to data sources.
column2:
A managed private endpoint connects a supported Fabric workload privately to a data source. The connection is outbound from the workload's perspective. Support varies by workload, so it is not a universal inbound privacy setting for Fabric.
Review source
